GEWORLD - The Contemporary World | Sjenica Sevilla, MA 
Term 1, A.Y. 2026-2027 
From Minerals to Microchips: The Global Biography of a GIGABYTE GeForce 
RTX 5070 WINDFORCE 
The object and its global significance 
 
Catalogue case 
WINDFORCE OC SFF 12G 
GV-N5070WF3OC-12GD 
12 GB GDDR7; 192-bit 
6,144 CUDA cores 
PCI Express 5.0 
(GIGABYTE, n.d.-c) 
Figure 1. Supplied PC photograph. GIGABYTE and GeForce RTX branding are visible; the 
model label is not. The catalogue variant above requires confirmation against the owned card. 
A graphics card appears to be a single purchase, yet its usefulness depends on resources, 
industrial skills and institutions spread across borders. This biography examines the stated 
RTX 5070 WINDFORCE object through the documented OC SFF catalogue model, without 
treating the photograph as proof of its exact variant. The central argument is that global value 
chains distribute production internationally while concentrating control over scarce 
knowledge and manufacturing capabilities. 
The chain runs from extraction and refining to chip fabrication, memory and board 
components, GIGABYTE integration, international distribution, Philippine use and eventual 
recovery or disposal. Globalization therefore joins consumers to distant labor and ecological 
consequences. The economic question is not simply where the card is made, but which actors 
create value, which can negotiate favorable terms, and which bear costs outside the sales 
transaction. 
Week 4 provides the main framework: production fragmentation makes this object possible, 
while its unequal rewards and responsibilities complicate the benefits of trade. Weeks 2, 3, 5 
and 6 illuminate interdependence, vulnerability, environmental limits and the coordination of 
specialized activities.

2 
From the earth to the silicon die 
The material chain begins before any chip exists. GIGABYTE confirms a copper cooling 
plate and composite copper heat pipes for this catalogue model (n.d.-b). Silicon is central to 
its semiconductor technology. Aluminum cooling structures, gold contacts, tin solder, 
tantalum capacitors and tungsten in semiconductor processes are relevant industry materials, 
but their exact presence, mass and suppliers in this board are not established by the published 
specifications. Published specifications therefore support only a partial material account. 
The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS, 2026) identifies Chile, the Democratic Republic of the 
Congo and Peru as major copper miners; China is a major silicon-metal and primary-
aluminum producer. Guinea and Australia are major bauxite producers, while China, 
Indonesia and Peru contribute tin; Congo and Rwanda contribute tantalum. Gold production 
includes China, Russia and Australia, and tungsten production is concentrated in China. 
These are possible upstream contexts, not the card’s traced origins. Silicon-metal output also 
differs from production of semiconductor-grade wafers. 
 
Figure 2. Material-to-chip transformation, simplified from USGS (2026) and OECD (2025). 
Arrows show processing stages, not verified country-to-country shipments. 
Refining changes mineral concentrates into usable materials; further purification, crystal 
growth and wafer preparation produce the substrate for circuits. NVIDIA designs the RTX 
5070’s GB205 GPU, manufactured using TSMC’s custom 4 nm 4N process (NVIDIA, 2025). 
Lithography and other repeated processing steps create circuits, followed by testing and 
packaging. Neither a particular fab nor a wafer lot can be identified for the pictured object. 
This is Week 2 interdependence with unequal substitutability: an abundant mineral cannot 
replace qualified wafers, equipment or fabrication knowledge. OECD (2025) distinguishes 
research-intensive design from capital-intensive fabrication. Entry requires more than low 
wages; it requires equipment, process expertise and reliable infrastructure. Week 3’s 
agricultural trade-shock framework helps explain concentrated supply and disruption risks, 
although chips differ from seasonal, perishable food and depend heavily on proprietary 
technology. 
Extraction supplies livelihoods and export earnings, but work can be hazardous. The 
International Labour Organization (ILO, 2019) documents child-labor risks in artisanal 
mining linked to global supply chains. This establishes a due-diligence concern, not an 
allegation about GIGABYTE’s particular suppliers. Traceability matters because a consumer 
cannot infer labor conditions from the finished product’s appearance.

3 
Components and the global production network 
The GPU die alone cannot function as a retail graphics card. The documented model 
combines 12 GB of GDDR7 memory, a circuit board, power-delivery components, 
connectors and cooling. GIGABYTE lists fans, thermal gel, a copper plate and heat pipes 
(n.d.-b, n.d.-c). Memory feeds data to the GPU; board circuitry connects components; voltage 
regulation supplies usable electrical power; the cooler removes heat. The exact memory 
maker, board supplier and component factories remain unverified. 
 
Figure 3. Selected production geographies, based on OECD (2025) and GIGABYTE (n.d.-a). 
Taiwan denotes the foundry sector, not a verified fab for this unit. No shipping route is 
shown. Basemap: Natural Earth (n.d.). 
NVIDIA provides the architecture and chip design; GIGABYTE integrates the GPU with 
supporting parts and sells the finished branded board. Corporate production lines are 
documented in Nanping, Taoyuan, and in Ningbo and Dongguan, China (GIGABYTE, n.d.-
a). This does not identify the photographed card’s final assembly site. A headquarters, 
foundry, packaging plant and board-assembly factory perform different activities and cannot 
be substituted for one another. 
At industry level, integration generally requires placing and soldering components on a 
printed circuit board, fitting the cooling assembly, and testing electrical and thermal 
performance. Specialized suppliers reduce the need for each firm to reproduce every 
capability. Yet dependence on qualified suppliers can also narrow bargaining options. OECD 
(2025) shows that design and fabrication generally occupy different value and profit positions 
from assembly, testing and packaging. Control over designs and scarce process expertise 
strengthens the bargaining position of NVIDIA and foundries. There is no verified 
breakdown of this card’s retail price or profits by actor. 
Ledezma’s (2017) fast-fashion analysis provides a useful Week 4 comparison: international 
production and replacement cycles connect consumption to distant work. Electronics, 
however, adds costly fabrication facilities and technical bottlenecks that prevent a simple 
apparel analogy. Week 6’s global-city lens concerns coordination: design teams, finance and 
business services connect dispersed activities. A factory cluster is not automatically a global 
city, and the evidence does not establish any individual worker’s migration history.

4 
Philippine consumption and global responsibility 
A Philippine retailer, DynaQuest PC (n.d.), lists the exact OC SFF catalogue SKU, 
establishing a local market channel. It does not establish where this particular card was 
bought. An illustrative distribution chain is an overseas production site, freight forwarder, 
Philippine importer and customs clearance, distributor or retailer, then consumer. The port, 
transport mode and intermediaries cannot be verified without transaction and freight records. 
A route through Taiwan, China or a regional hub cannot be inferred from the local retail 
listing. 
Importing an advanced graphics card coexists with Philippine industrial participation. OECD 
(2024) identifies domestic strengths in semiconductor assembly, testing and packaging. This 
does not prove Philippine participation in this RTX 5070’s production. It does show why the 
country should be understood as both a consumer market and a production economy. 
Retailing, repair and creative work can generate local value, while access to advanced 
designs and fabrication remains internationally dependent. 
Gaming, video production, 3D work and compatible AI tasks are potential uses, rather than 
verified personal habits (NVIDIA, 2025). For a Filipino consumer, access can support digital 
participation, but a purchase also creates electricity and replacement costs. As an illustration, 
NVIDIA’s 250 W reference graphics-power figure implies 22.5 kWh at a constant 250 W for 
three hours daily over 30 days. This is a calculation, not measured use of the owned card; 
total computer consumption and actual workloads differ. 
Week 5’s concern with environmental limits extends beyond tourism: consumption draws on 
finite resources and waste-management capacity. A complete footprint would include 
extraction, fabrication, freight, use and disposal; no verified lifecycle total for this exact card 
is available. The World Health Organization (WHO, 2024) reports 62 million tonnes of 
global e-waste in 2022, with only 22.3% documented as formally collected and recycled. 
These are historical global figures, not Philippine graphics-card statistics. Unsafe disposal 
can expose communities to hazardous substances. 
Responsible consumption therefore includes maintaining airflow, obtaining qualified repair 
when feasible, extending useful service and transferring a functional card for reuse. At end of 
life, an owner should verify a collection program’s downstream recycler rather than assume 
any collection bin guarantees recovery. These choices do not replace supplier accountability 
or public regulation. They link consumer decisions to the welfare of workers and 
communities beyond the household. 
The card’s biography reveals a global economy held together by specialization and marked 
by unequal control. Its benefits reach a Philippine desk because miners, engineers, factory 
workers and service providers contribute different kinds of value. Global citizenship means 
recognizing those relationships, demanding better evidence about their costs, and treating 
ownership as an ongoing responsibility rather than the end of the supply chain.
